title: Base vs total comp
real: Candidates compare base salary to base salary because it's the only number that's easy to hold in your head. Bonus, equity, pension contribution and benefits get waved away as 'nice to have'. Often the offer is genuinely competitive on total and weak on base, and the candidate hasn't clocked it. Sometimes the opposite: their current bonus is mostly theoretical and they're overvaluing it. Before anyone negotiates, get both packages written down side by side. You're not trying to talk them out of their concern. You're making sure the concern is real.
ladder: What did your bonus actually pay out the last two years, not the target, the real number?
If we lined both packages up on one page, which line would you want to see move first?
How much of the equity are you counting as real money today?
watch: If they light up about equity, check they understand vesting and the strike price. Excitement now becomes regret at the offer stage.
text:
# Base vs total comp

> MOCK DATA. Written for the Caddy Lab prototype to stand in for a real recruiting best-practice corpus.

## What's really going on

Candidates compare base salary to base salary because it's the only number that's easy to hold in your head. Bonus, equity, pension contribution and benefits get waved away as 'nice to have'. Often the offer is genuinely competitive on total and weak on base, and the candidate hasn't clocked it. Sometimes the opposite: their current bonus is mostly theoretical and they're overvaluing it. Before anyone negotiates, get both packages written down side by side. You're not trying to talk them out of their concern. You're making sure the concern is real.

## Dig deeper

1. What did your bonus actually pay out the last two years, not the target, the real number?
2. If we lined both packages up on one page, which line would you want to see move first?
3. How much of the equity are you counting as real money today?

## Watch for

If they light up about equity, check they understand vesting and the strike price. Excitement now becomes regret at the offer stage.

title: Bonus or vesting cliff
real: Candidates close to a bonus payout or vesting cliff will quietly drag their feet. It's rational. Get the date and the amount on the table early, so the client can decide whether to buy it out or wait. Hiding it until offer stage kills deals.
ladder: When does your bonus pay out, and roughly how much are we talking?
Is there any equity vesting in the next six months?
If the client covered that, or timed your start after it, does the timing worry go away?
watch: Buyouts are more common than candidates think. Ask the client before assuming no.

title: Candidate going quiet
real: When a candidate stops replying, it's rarely because they're busy. They're usually talking to someone else, having doubts, or embarrassed about saying no. Make it easy for them to tell you the truth.
ladder: Has anything changed since we last spoke?
Is there something about the role you've been unsure how to bring up?
Would it be easier if I just asked: are you still interested?
watch: Give people an easy out. The ones who take it were going to leave anyway.

title: Career direction
real: When a candidate talks about where they want to be in three years, listen for whether this role is a step on that path or a detour. People will take a detour for money, but they don't stay. Map the path out loud with them and be honest about where this role sits.
ladder: Where do you want to be in three years, and what's the step that gets you there?
Does this role move you closer to that, or is it a side step?
What would you need to learn in the next job to make that jump?
watch: Candidates who want leadership but are being pitched an IC role are a classic mismatch. Name it early.

ladder: What have you been telling yourself about the silence?
Are other processes moving while you wait?
If I can get you an answer by Thursday, will you hold until then?
watch: Silence from the client for more than a week is a deal risk. Chase internally before the candidate chases you.

title: Buying signal
real: When a candidate says 'that sounds great' or asks about next steps, stop selling. Most recruiters keep talking and talk themselves out of the deal. Confirm the interest, surface any last objection, and lock the next step with a date.
ladder: On a scale of one to ten, where are you right now, and what would make it a ten?
Is there anything that would stop you saying yes if an offer came through?
Can we lock in the next conversation before we hang up?
watch: A six or seven is a real answer. Ask what the missing points are, that's your remaining objection.

title: Comp gap
real: When a candidate says the number is low, nine times out of ten they haven't done the maths on the whole package yet, or they're anchoring to a figure someone else gave them. The worst move is jumping straight to the client to ask for more. You lose credibility with both sides and you still don't know what the real gap is. Your job is to find out three things: the number they actually need, the number they'd love, and where that number came from. Those are rarely the same figure. A candidate who says 'I need 180' often means 'my mate at a bigger company is on 180 and I'd feel silly taking less'. That's an ego gap, not a mortgage gap, and you handle it completely differently.
ladder: When you say it's lower than you hoped, what number did you have in your head, and where did that number come from?
If the base landed exactly where you want, what else about this role would still give you pause?
What's the number where you'd stop thinking about money and start thinking about the work?
If I went back to them with that, and they got close but not all the way, what would make the difference for you?
watch: Candidates who won't name a number are usually using another offer as the anchor. Pivot to the competing process ladder.

title: Company stability

title: Competing process
real: When a candidate mentions another process, they're usually doing one of three things: genuinely telling you the timeline, creating urgency to get a better number, or quietly preparing you for a no. You need to know which. Don't panic and don't get competitive about the other company. Get curious. The single most valuable fact is what they like about the other role that this one doesn't have. That's the real objection, and it's often not money at all.
ladder: Where are you with them, honestly, and what's the next step and date?
What do they have that this role doesn't, if you had to name one thing?
If both offers landed on the same day with the same number, which would you pick and why?
What would this client need to do this week to stay in the running?
watch: If they can't name anything the other role does better, the other process is leverage, not a threat. Handle it as a comp conversation.

title: Counteroffer risk
real: Counteroffers are the most common way an accepted offer dies. If the candidate mentions their manager would 'probably match', assume they will, and assume the candidate is half considering it. The research every recruiter quotes is that most people who accept a counter leave within a year anyway, but quoting that sounds self-serving. Instead, get them to say out loud why they started looking. If money alone fixes that reason, you have a real risk.
ladder: What made you start looking in the first place? Go back to the very first moment.
If they matched the money tomorrow, would that reason go away?
How do you think your manager would react when you hand your notice in?
What would you say to them if they offered a promotion to stay?
watch: Rehearse the resignation conversation before the offer is signed, not after.

title: Equity skepticism
real: Plenty of candidates have been burned by options that went to zero. When they say 'equity is just paper', they're telling you about their last company, not this one. Don't argue the upside. Ask what would make it feel real. The answer tells you whether you're dealing with risk aversion, a cash flow need, or a story they've heard. Cash flow needs are solvable with base. Risk aversion is a fit question.
ladder: Was there a past company where equity didn't work out for you? What happened?
If you knew the equity was worth zero, would the base on its own still work?
What would you need to know about the company to start counting it?
watch: A candidate with a mortgage and young kids saying this is usually a base problem dressed up as an equity problem.

title: Exploding offer
real: An offer with a hard deadline is a pressure tactic, and candidates know it, but it still works on them. Your job is to slow the decision down without looking like you're stalling for your client. Find out whether the deadline is real, whether they've asked for more time, and how they actually feel about the other company once you take the clock away.
ladder: Is that deadline firm, or have you asked them for more time yet?
If the deadline wasn't there, would you take that offer today?
What would you want to have seen from us before Friday to feel good either way?
watch: Candidates who'd say yes without the deadline are gone. Spend your energy on the ones who hesitate.

title: Hiring manager fit
real: People join companies and leave managers. If a candidate didn't click with the hiring manager, that's the most important thing they'll say on the call. Find out whether it was style, a bad day, or a values clash. A bad day can be fixed with a second conversation. A values clash can't.
ladder: What specifically didn't land, was it something they said or how they said it?
What's the best manager you've had like, compared to them?
Would a second, more informal conversation with them help?
If you had a different manager in the same role, would you take it?
watch: If they'd take the role with a different manager, the role is fine and the manager isn't. Tell the client gently.

If I could get a decision this week, would that change anything?

title: Motivation mismatch
real: Lukewarm language is the loudest signal on a call and the easiest to miss. 'I guess', 'it's fine', 'could be OK' all mean the role doesn't connect to what they actually want. Don't sell harder. Selling a lukewarm candidate gets you an accept followed by a no-show or a three month leaver. Find out what would make them excited, then honestly decide whether this role does it. Sometimes the right move is to park them and come back with the right job. That trust pays off later.
ladder: When you picture your next role going really well, what are you doing on a Tuesday afternoon?
What part of this role, if any, actually got your attention?
What would have to be true about this job for you to be genuinely excited, not just OK with it?
If this isn't it, what should I be looking for on your behalf?
watch: If their answer to the first question describes a different job, say so. You'll be the first recruiter who has.

title: Timing objection
real: 'Now's not the right time' is usually a polite no or a real constraint, and you have to work out which without being pushy. Real constraints have dates attached: a bonus in March, a vest in June, a wedding in August. Polite nos are vague. If there's a date, work back from it and see if the client can flex. If it's vague, the objection is something else and timing is the cover story.
ladder: What specifically makes now tricky? Is there a date you're waiting for?
If that date had already passed, would you be moving on this?
What would need to happen between now and then for you to be ready?
Would it help if the start date was set around that?
watch: No date usually means no interest. Gently ask what would make it the right time, then listen for the real objection.

title: Title concerns
real: Title objections come from three places: how it looks on LinkedIn, how it affects the next job search, and pride. All three are valid. Find out which, then check what the title actually means at this client. A 'Senior' at a 40 person startup can be broader than a 'Lead' at a bank. Sometimes the client will flex the title for free, it costs them nothing.
ladder: Is it how it looks externally, or what it says about your scope?
What title would you need to see, and why that one?
If the scope and pay were right, how much would the title still matter?
Would it help if I asked whether the title is flexible?
watch: Title is one of the cheapest things for a client to give. Ask early.

title: Trial close
real: A trial close checks commitment without asking for the final yes. Use it after every major objection is handled, so you're never surprised at the offer stage.
ladder: If they came back with that number, would you accept it?
Is there anyone else who needs to be comfortable with this before you say yes?
What would you say to them if they called you tomorrow with an offer?
watch: Hesitation on a trial close is gold. It means there's an objection left, and you found it early.
